facts.text: ROC curves and DET curves show how a detector's misses and false alarms trade off as its sensitivity setting changes.
facts.quote: A ROC curve and a DET curve are graphs that show how a detector's misses and false alarms trade against each other as its sensitivity setting is turned up or down.

facts.text: The booklet lists choosing a ROC, DET or precision-recall operating point as a detector tuning method that is simple, transparent and standard.
facts.quote: The booklet lists "ROC, DET or precision-recall operating point" as one tuning method: simple, transparent and standard for detectors

facts.text: Choosing a ROC, DET or precision-recall operating point tunes only the detector threshold, ignores closed-loop timing and braking, and serves a single objective.
facts.quote: but it tunes the threshold alone, ignores closed-loop timing and braking, and serves a single objective

facts.text: A detector's ROC, DET or precision-recall operating point should be chosen on a validation split and followed by closed-loop evaluation.
facts.quote: the point should be chosen on a validation split and followed by closed-loop evaluation [Chapter 9]

facts.text: Detector false alarms should be measured by exposure, per hour or per maneuver, because of the trade-off between misses and false alarms.
facts.quote: The same trade-off is why false alarms should be measured by exposure, per hour or per maneuver

facts.text: Operators will reject a detector tuned never to miss if the detector alarms constantly.
facts.quote: a detector tuned never to miss will be rejected by operators if it alarms constantly [Chapters 4, 7]

facts.text: For an automatic brake, misses and false alarms carry very different costs, and the right detector operating point depends on speed, zone and task.
facts.quote: For an automatic brake the two axes carry very different costs, and the right operating point depends on speed, zone and task

facts.text: The booklet frames automatic-brake tuning as pursuing several goals simultaneously under hard safety constraints, with the detector curve serving as one input.
facts.quote: the booklet frames the real tuning problem as several goals at once under hard safety constraints, with the detector curve as one input [Chapter 9]
